title: Arrays and Slices
summary: Store fixed-size data in arrays and growing data in slices with append and make, then slice, join, and sort them.
intro: Most programs work with lists of values. Go gives you two tools: arrays, which have a fixed length and copy on assignment, and slices, which grow with `append` and share their elements. You will use slices nearly everywhere, so this lesson ends with cutting, joining, and sorting them.

steps.title: Arrays
steps.body:
An array holds a fixed number of values of one type. `[5]int` means exactly five ints, and that length never changes. Write the values in a literal, or use `[...]` to let the compiler count them:

```go
days := [3]string{"mon", "tue", "wed"}
laps := [...]int{62, 59, 61} // type is [3]int
var counts [4]int           // [0 0 0 0]
```

A new array starts with zero values, so `counts` holds four zeros. Read and write with `a[i]`, counting from 0. `len(a)` gives the length, so the last element is `a[len(a)-1]`. An index past the end does not compile when it is a constant, and panics at run time otherwise.

Arrays are values. `b := a` copies every element into new memory, so changing `b` leaves `a` alone. The length is part of the type: `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different types and cannot be assigned to each other. `fmt.Println` prints an array as `[1 2 3]`.

example.title: Temperature backup
example.prompt: Store five temperatures in an array, fix one, copy the array, and show that the copy is independent.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	temps := [5]int{18, 21, 19, 24, 22}
	temps[2] = 20

	backup := temps
	backup[0] = 0

	fmt.Println("temps:", temps)
	fmt.Println("backup:", backup)
	fmt.Println("days:", len(temps))
	fmt.Println("last:", temps[len(temps)-1])

	var counts [3]int
	fmt.Println("counts:", counts)
}
example.explanation: `temps[2] = 20` overwrites the third value. `backup := temps` copies all five ints, so `backup[0] = 0` changes only the copy and `temps` still starts with 18. `temps[len(temps)-1]` is `temps[4]`, the last element. `counts` was never given values, so it holds three zeros.

practice.title: Lap times
practice.prompt:
Record four lap times in an array, fix the last one, and make an independent copy.

1. Keep the given `laps := [...]int{62, 59, 61, 60}` and remove the placeholder lines.
2. Change the last lap to 58 using `laps[len(laps)-1]`.
3. Copy the array with `best := laps`, then set `best[1] = 57`.
4. Print `laps:` and `laps`, then `best:` and `best`, then `count:` and `len(laps)`.
5. Declare `var pits [2]int` without values and print `pits:` and `pits`.

Expected output:

```text
laps: [62 59 61 58]
best: [62 57 61 58]
count: 4
pits: [0 0]
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	laps := [...]int{62, 59, 61, 60}
	laps[len(laps)-1] = 58

	best := laps
	best[1] = 57

	fmt.Println("laps:", laps)
	fmt.Println("best:", best)
	fmt.Println("count:", len(laps))

	var pits [2]int
	fmt.Println("pits:", pits)
}
hints: Change `best` only after copying, so `laps` keeps 59 at index 1.
`var pits [2]int` needs no values: a new array starts with zeros.

steps.title: Slices
steps.body:
A slice is a list that can grow. Its type has no length: `[]string`. Real Go code uses slices far more than arrays.

```go
cart := []string{"milk"}
cart = append(cart, "eggs")       // one value
cart = append(cart, "jam", "tea") // several at once
```

`append` returns the new slice, so always assign it back. Writing `append(cart, "eggs")` alone does not compile, because the result is unused. A nil slice (`var ids []int`) has length 0 and works with `append` right away, so there is no need to create it first.

`make([]int, n)` makes a slice of `n` zero values that you can index straight away. `len(s)` is the current number of elements.

Gotcha: a slice does not hold its elements. It is a small view that points at them in memory. `alias := cart` copies the view, not the elements, so both names share the same values and a change to an element through one shows through the other. That is the opposite of arrays, where assignment copies every element. Do not count on this after an `append`, though: it may move the elements to new memory, which a later lesson explains.

example.title: Shopping cart
example.prompt: Grow a cart with append, show that a second name shares its items, and make a slice of zeros.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	cart := []string{"milk", "eggs"}
	cart = append(cart, "bread")
	cart = append(cart, "jam", "tea")
	fmt.Println(cart, len(cart))

	alias := cart
	alias[0] = "oat milk"
	fmt.Println(cart)

	qty := make([]int, 3)
	qty[1] = 2
	fmt.Println(qty)
}
example.output:
[milk eggs bread jam tea] 5
[oat milk eggs bread jam tea]
[0 2 0]
example.explanation: Each `append` returns a longer slice, which is stored back in `cart`. `alias := cart` does not copy the five strings: both names see the same elements, so changing `alias[0]` changes `cart[0]` too. `make([]int, 3)` gives `[0 0 0]`, and `qty[1] = 2` fills the middle one.

practice.title: Playlist
practice.prompt:
Build a playlist from an empty slice, then show that a second name shares its songs.

1. Remove the placeholder lines. Starting from `var playlist []string`, append `Intro`, `Rise`, and `Echo` one at a time, then `Drift` and `Glow` in one call.
2. Print `playlist` and its length on one line.
3. Set `shared := playlist`, change `shared[4]` to `Dawn`, and print `playlist`.
4. Make `plays := make([]int, 4)`, set its last element to 9, and print it.

Expected output:

```text
[Intro Rise Echo Drift Glow] 5
[Intro Rise Echo Drift Dawn]
[0 0 0 9]
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var playlist []string
	playlist = append(playlist, "Intro")
	playlist = append(playlist, "Rise")
	playlist = append(playlist, "Echo")
	playlist = append(playlist, "Drift", "Glow")
	fmt.Println(playlist, len(playlist))

	shared := playlist
	shared[4] = "Dawn"
	fmt.Println(playlist)

	plays := make([]int, 4)
	plays[len(plays)-1] = 9
	fmt.Println(plays)
}

tests.output:
[Intro Rise Echo Drift Glow] 5
[Intro Rise Echo Drift Dawn]
[0 0 0 9]

hints: Write `playlist = append(playlist, "Intro")`. A nil slice is fine to append to.
Pass two values to one `append` call for Drift and Glow.

steps.title: Slicing and joining
steps.body:
`s[low:high]` takes a piece of a slice: it includes index `low` and stops before `high`, so it has `high - low` elements. Leave out either end to mean the start or the end:

```go
s := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
fmt.Println(s[1:3])       // [20 30]
fmt.Println(s[:2])        // first two: [10 20]
fmt.Println(s[len(s)-2:]) // last two: [40 50]
s = s[:len(s)-1]          // drop the last: [10 20 30 40]
```

To join two slices, spread the second one into `append` with `...`: `a = append(a, b...)`. Without the dots, Go tries to append the whole slice as one element and the program does not compile.

Gotchas: a slice expression does not copy anything. The piece shares its elements with the original, so writing to `s[1:3][0]` changes `s[1]`. Keep both bounds between 0 and `len(s)`. Going past the length does not always panic. After you drop an element, `s[:len(s)+1]` quietly brings it back, so treat `len(s)` as the limit.

example.title: Score ranges
example.prompt: Print the lowest two, top three, and middle scores, then drop the last score and join two new ones.
example.explanation: `scores[:2]` is indexes 0 and 1. `scores[len(scores)-3:]` starts at index 2 and runs to the end. `scores[1:4]` takes indexes 1, 2, and 3 but not 4. Reslicing to `len(scores)-1` drops 95, and `append(scores, extra...)` adds both values from `extra` in order.

practice.title: Name list
practice.prompt:
Take pieces of a list of names, then drop the last name and join two more.

1. Keep the given `names` and `more`, and remove the placeholder lines. Print `first:` and the first three names.
2. Print `last:` and the last two names, using `len(names)`.
3. Print `middle:` and `names[1:3]`.
4. Drop the last name, join `[]string{"Zed", "Kim"}` onto the end with `...`, and print `joined:` and `names`.

Expected output:

```text
first: [Ava Eve Leo]
last: [Max Tom]
middle: [Eve Leo]
joined: [Ava Eve Leo Max Zed Kim]
```

tests.output:
first: [Ava Eve Leo]
last: [Max Tom]
middle: [Eve Leo]
joined: [Ava Eve Leo Max Zed Kim]

hints: Drop the last with `names = names[:len(names)-1]`, then `names = append(names, more...)`.

steps.title: Sorting

example.title: Sorted results
example.prompt: Sort a slice of ints, floats, and strings in place, then print the lowest and highest score.
example.explanation: Each sort function rearranges its slice in place, so printing the same variables afterwards shows the sorted order. `Apple` comes first because uppercase `A` has a smaller byte value than any lowercase letter. Once `scores` is sorted, the ends of the slice are the lowest and highest scores.

practice.title: Sorted lists
practice.prompt:
Sort three slices and report the lightest and heaviest weight.

1. Add `"sort"` to the imports and remove the placeholder lines.
2. Sort `laps`, `weights`, and `cities` in place with the matching sort function.
3. Print each slice on its own line.
4. Print `lightest:` and `heaviest:` with the smallest and largest weight, formatted with `%.2f`.

Expected output:

```text
[58 59 61 64]
[0.75 1.5 2.5]
[Oslo lima rome]
lightest: 0.75
heaviest: 2.50
```
hints: Use `sort.Ints`, `sort.Float64s`, and `sort.Strings`, each on its own line.
After sorting, the lightest is `weights[0]` and the heaviest is `weights[len(weights)-1]`.

recap:
- `[N]T` is an array: fixed length, zero values to start, and assignment copies every element.
- `[]T` is a slice: grow it with `s = append(s, x)`, always assigning the result back, and make zeros with `make([]T, n)`.
- Assigning a slice shares its elements, it does not copy them.
- `s[low:high]` includes `low` and excludes `high`. Join with `append(a, b...)`.
- `sort.Ints`, `sort.Float64s`, and `sort.Strings` sort in place, uppercase before lowercase.
